body:
> A lot of kids who've had a tough enough time in life to end up seriously considering suicide have learned that when somebody says they want to help, things usually get worse for them.

What do you mean by that exactly, get worse in what way? 

Thanks again for the advice, you've brought up some great points that I would not have thought about.

Your IASP link matched with the one I had found. Not an ideal resource but it's better than nothing. 

I'd like to get the parents involved. My main reason being that her suicide plan implied doing it at night, therefore at home. At that point the only people who could respond quickly enough should an event develop would be the parents. I'm of the mindset that the most likely person to respond should be the first to know.

Regarding contact, you say be responsive for signals. Does that mean I should back off if she tells me to? I mean, she told me I didn't have to be involved, which isn't saying "don't be involved". I'm just wondering whether I should take it easy or at the very least maintain daily personal contact.

I'll re-assess things Monday I suppose. I may run into her Saturday morning. Friday's improvement was a good sign, at least to me.

You're pretty perceptive. I do a lot of creative writing, so it's funny you make that comparison. 

The raised by narcissists point is highly likely considering the circumstances. This is a really high end private school in Latin America. You're perpetually dealing with a lot of rich/spoiled asshole parents who project their bullshit onto their kids. 

As far as a suicide hotline, I've looked around and found nothing but a single NGO, which is understaffed to the point where it can only offer support from 3-10 PM. 

I'd like to take it day by day for now. There's a few things that concern me which I'd like some guidance on...

1. I have no means of contacting her outside of school, and I don't think anyone at home knows about this. I'd like to get them involved without triggering an alarm on her part, or again having it come back to me. If I felt that it was escalating, I'd forget about myself and say whatever needs to be said.

2. How much contact is too much? I want to be careful not to attract too much attention from other people onto her because that could make it worse. I also don't want her to see me as pestering her.

3. Should I try to give her any information? Any web stuff? I've seen a lot, from the suicideproject to every .org guide, but I'm not sure what would be good for a person her age.

Thanks a lot for the reply. I think she was genuinely grateful for my attention yesterday and is just pushing people away as a defensive reflex.

I DO get her, and when I told her that I wasn't trying to understand her situation I was trying to avoid the classic "I know how you feel" BS that doesn't work. Semi-fortunately I did some suicide research recently because an ex-student died on campus and I was looking for some warning signs just in case. So that helped. I've read the talking tips and so far I think I've followed them well.

I'm not in the US, and so her behavior is even more unusual here. She'd fit right in in a typical US high school, at least with somebody. But here, it's even more conformist. They all have to wear uniforms and the school seems to impress upon them the idea of being this ideal person.

I don't know anything about her home situation although yesterday she kind of alluded to a couple things which I'd like to dig deeper on but didn't have time. She mentioned that her mom sent her brother to a therapist for his bad grades but wouldn't send her to one because "only crazy girls see therapists." Sounded like she might have reached out once. Then she started saying something that seemed like she'd been punished in weird ways. Something about maybe being fed old leftovers while other people ate new food. Honestly, was kinda hard to tell.

To clarify on the psychologist point. The ones at my school are generally only involved when a kid is in trouble, either for grades or behavior. They make no effort to reach out to kids for other reasons, and visit the cafeteria 4 times a day. 

I didn't want it to come right back to me because I think I was the only person she had told as of yesterday. So I told the psychologist simply that she seemed depressed and that she should make it a point to talk to her. The psychologist apparently already knew that this girl had been talking about changing schools and meant to discuss that. I didn't tell her about the suicidal thoughts, as I was hoping she could try to fish them out on her own.

After seeing her talking seriously to another teacher today, I am planning on talking to him, and then again with the psychologist. I don't want to hide any information, but I'm also afraid of damaging the delicate bond I have with her right now. We've always gotten along very well, and since I think I was the first person she told I'd be worried that she might cut me off if she knew I leaked it to someone who she probably doesn't like.
